body: TL;DR Samsung is reportedly considering an end to major OS upgrades on older Galaxy Watches. According to the leaker, the security update schedule will continue as planned. Some watches have overheated so much that they’ve caused burns on the wrists of those who wear them. title: Trump Phone passes the bend test, fails the originality test
summary: The gold paint can only hide so much.
body: TL;DR JerryRigEverything puts the Trump Mobile T1 through scratch, bend, and teardown tests, with the phone surviving the physical punishment. The teardown reveals internals identical to the two-year-old HTC U24 Pro, reinforcing earlier findings from an iFixit investigation. Swapping the motherboards between the two phones leaves both fully functional, further proving their shared hardware origins. Buying a phone is one thing. Watching someone scratch, bend, and rip it apart is an entirely different kind of satisfaction. The Trump Mobile T1 Phone has finally received that treatment from JerryRigEverything, and while it holds up surprisingly well against physical abuse, its insides tell a far less flattering story. YouTuber Zack Nelson put the gold-colored handset through his usual durability tests, starting with the display, which scratches at level six on the Mohs hardness scale, with deeper grooves appearing at level seven. That’s fairly standard for a modern smartphone. The metal frame also checks out, and despite attempts to bend the device from both directions, the T1 Phone survives without snapping or suffering an obvious structural failure.

title: The next big threat to RCS isn’t another messaging app
summary: The clock is ticking for RCS as AI threatens to rewrite the rules of messaging.
body: TL;DR The GSMA warns that the next six to twelve months could determine whether RCS leads the shift toward AI-powered conversations or follows rival platforms. Despite billions of daily RCS messages, commercial adoption remains relatively small, with the technology still largely focused on notifications. The GSMA is developing new conversational capabilities, but hasn’t announced specific features or release timelines. Six to twelve months. That’s how long the GSMA believes RCS has to establish itself as a serious player in the next era of messaging , or risk watching AI-powered conversations and rival platforms define that future without it. It’s an unusually urgent warning from the organization responsible for the messaging standard, especially as RCS adoption accelerates. But the concern isn’t whether people will continue sending messages. It’s whether those messages can do more than simply deliver information in a world where AI assistants are increasingly capable of acting on it .

Google is also introducing multi-turn ads in the US, allowing sponsored results to appear during follow-up questions in AI Mode. Google’s AI Mode is meant to make web searches easier. You ask a question, it pulls information from different websites, and you get a detailed answer without opening a dozen tabs. But as more people turn to AI Mode for everyday searches, Google is also finding new ways to show them ads. And if you’ve been enjoying an ad-free experience in AI Mode outside the US, that’s about to change. Google has announced that ads in AI Mode are expanding to 10 more countries, including India, Australia, Canada, Kenya, Malaysia, New Zealand, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Singapore. The company also plans to bring them to Brazil, Mexico, and the UK later in Q4 2026.

body: Google Messages is one of our clear favorites when it comes to Android messaging solutions, but even Google doesn’t get everything right. Over the years, the messaging platform has introduced a lot that has gone right, including RCS, end-to-end encryption, and newer features like Scam Detection . But not every single addition has been a home run. Last month, we asked you how you feel about the app’s ever-growing feature set, and which ones are your least favorite. As it turns out, you had a clear favorite when it came to picking your least favorite . The poll in question was part of an article highlighting Google Messages features that we turn off , and it attracted 1,144 votes. And while it offered five different options to choose from, and a sixth option for anything we might have missed, one feature managed to get almost 50% of the votes: the Gemini button.

title: Samsung’s open-ear Galaxy Buds On are coming to the US, and we finally know when
summary: US availability starts next week!
body: TL;DR Samsung’s first open-ear earbuds, the Galaxy Buds On, are coming to the US on November 6 for $229. The clip-style earbuds feature sound leakage reduction, up to 9.5 hours of battery life, wireless charging, and Gemini Live support. The Galaxy Buds On lack ANC and Bluetooth multipoint support, and come in just one size and color. After trying an all-new aspect ratio for its foldable earlier this year, Samsung is also betting on a new earbud design. The South Korean company has stuck to familiar earbud designs in the past, but that’s changing now with the Galaxy Buds On. The tech giant launched the new open-ear Galaxy Buds On in Korea yesterday, and even though they aren’t immediately available in the US, the wait for their eventual availability won’t be long. Samsung has confirmed that the Galaxy Buds On will go on sale stateside on November 6, and they’ll cost $229. That’s just a little over a week to wait at this point.

title: Bank of America is begging customers not to hand their passwords to AI assistants
summary: AI agents are getting smarter, but banks aren't ready to hand them the vault keys.
body: TL;DR Bank of America is warning customers not to share banking usernames or passwords with AI assistants and agents. Customers could be held responsible for activity resulting from voluntarily granting an AI agent account access, subject to applicable consumer protections. As Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, and other AI assistants become more autonomous, banks are increasingly concerned about unauthorized access and liability. AI assistants can write your emails, book appointments, shop on your behalf, and increasingly handle tasks you’d rather not do yourself. It’s the kind of convenience that’s hard to resist, even as questions grow about how much access we’re giving these tools . However, letting an AI assistant manage your calendar is one thing. Trusting it with your life savings is quite another, and Bank of America would rather its customers didn’t find out the hard way. The banking giant has emailed customers asking them not to share their banking credentials with AI assistants or agents. It’s a curious warning from a company that, in the same message, celebrates its investments in AI to make banking easier, more personalized, and more secure.
